body: @jrudolph thats interesting... I wonder where the 58 bytes come from. Any idea ?

@normanmaurer sorry for the delay... Here's a reproducer: https://github.com/netty/netty/compare/4.1...jrudolph:5976-test-case

I couldn't reproduce the number above exactly. Instead, I found that the number of output buffer space depends on the number of input bytes. I guess the reason is that the openssl engine tries to output all outstanding data for several frames in one go.

@jrudolph thanks a lot! I will open a PR with a fix for the other reported issue today. Maybe this will also fix this one :) Can you please confirm you grant me the right to include your test-code and so publish it under the ASL2 license as part of netty ?
Yes, I confirm that you can take the code under ASL2 license.

@jrudolph I think that it fails is kind of expected as `OpenSslEngine` will return `18668`and `SSLEngineImpl` will return `16921` from `session.getSession().getPacketBufferSize()`. The difference exists as the `OpenSslEngine` also supports compression (if openssl was compiled with support for it) while the JDK implementation does not so has no need to account for the maximum overhead of it for a record. That said I wonder if we can detect if compression should be used or not and depending on this "select" the correct value.

Makes sense ?

Hmm I thought `session.getSession().getPacketBufferSize()` would be about the output side, i.e. the second argument of the `wrap` call. The hard coded number in the test is the amount of data going into the `wrap` call.

So, the difference is that for `SslEngineImpl` the amount of output for a `wrap` call is always <= `getPacketBufferSize` while the `OpenSslEngine` will return `BUFFER_OVERFLOW` depending on the amount of input data.
@jrudolph ah sorry I misread the test-code. Let me check again... Stay tuned.
